turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Obs are done, I'll stay a tick in case the numbers come up.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lovely. What's brought you in?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Um, it's this cough. Every morning. And I'm, I'm frightened it's something really bad.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. How long have you had it?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Years, honestly. Years. Err, worse when I get up, with this brown phlegm. Not loads.
[SEG0006] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He's been clearing it into the sink since I started last spring. Same brown stuff.
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): I quit the fags last year, in the March. Twenty a day before that. Why's the cough still here if I stopped?
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Quitting doesn't undo it overnight, I'm afraid. Any chest pain when you cough?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. I keep checking with my hand, which is silly.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not silly. Weight, has that dropped?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): No, steady. I was 78 kilos last time. And I put the little finger machine on at home, it said 93. Do I need hospital for 93?
[SEG0012] person_1 (NURSE): Those home ones drift. Just now on ours, oxygen saturation 97 percent, pulse 78, weight 78.4 kilograms.
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): 97. Oh. So not hospital. Sorry, I spiral a bit.

[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me think out loud. Long smoking history, stopped last March, morning cough, brown phlegm, weight steady, no pain, clinic oxygen fine. That pattern is chronic bronchitis far more than anything nasty.
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Is bronchitis COPD? Is COPD cancer? I know that's a daft question.

[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not cancer. Err, COPD is narrowed airways after years of smoke, and the cough and phlegm is the bronchitis side. I won't call it COPD until we've measured you. I'm booking spirometry.
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): What actually happens? Does the tube hurt?
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): You blow hard down a tube, a few tries. No pain. They'll send you a slot.
[SEG0019] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Can I add what I've noticed? Cut on his shin healed in five days, nice and clean. But he sleeps badly, up and pacing.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Healed in five days means no slow-healing wounds, that's fine. Sleep I want to hear about.
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't sleep badly. I sleep fine. She's, um, fussing. Once for the loo and I'm gone again.
[SEG0022] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Also the water tablet. He doesn't take it on Sundays. Blister pack doesn't lie.
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): No, not Sundays. Saturdays. I miss Saturdays at my daughter's. Sunday I always take it.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Saturdays then, not Sundays. What strength is the water tablet?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): 2.5 milligrams every morning. They call it bendrofluazide. White, tiny. Except the Saturday.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bendroflumethiazide, yes, 2.5 mg once a morning, for the blood pressure. And the purple inhaler, still on that?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Two puffs, morning and night. I call it seratide, might be saying it wrong.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Seretide. Purple inhaler, fluticasone with salmeterol, two puffs twice daily. What about the blue one?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Salbutamol, the blue inhaler, when I'm wheezy. Maybe twice a week. Is that too much? Be straight with me.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Twice a week's modest. Any drug allergies?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): My brother's on metformin, he's diabetic. My sister takes biotin for her hair and she wants me on it for the cough. Would it help, even a bit?
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Biotin's hers, metformin's his. Not yours, and biotin won't shift this cough, so leave it. I'll note your brother's diabetes in the family history only.
[SEG0034] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I take a statin for my cholesterol. Nearly got written on his repeat once, so I'm saying it out loud.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stays off his list. The blood pressure, still ongoing?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, years. That's why the water tablet. You didn't check the pressure today, did you? Should you?
[SEG0037] person_1 (NURSE): No blood pressure this morning. Weight, pulse and oxygen only.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Another day for that. Any fever?
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): No fever.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Blood in the phlegm, ever?
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Brown, not red. Brown isn't secret blood, is it? I need you to say.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): It isn't. Old tarry phlegm looks brown. Fresh blood looks red or pink. Are you breathless?
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): A bit, on hills. Flat ground I'm okay if I go steady. That's the bad sign, isn't it?

[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): It fits, it doesn't prove disaster. Working impression, provisional, chronic bronchitis, and I can't exclude early COPD till the spirometry. If the numbers are down we might do a chest x-ray. Not ordering it today.
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): So x-ray is only if. Spirometry is actually booked? What if there's a shadow and we've waited?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Spirometry is booked. I'm not expecting a shadow. No blood, steady weight, no pain. This is not how a lung cancer story usually starts.
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): Chemist said a pneumonia jab, and flu, because I smoked. Do I need both? When?

[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'd advise both, pneumococcal and the yearly flu jab. You arrange them at the nurse clinic, I'm not injecting you now. Come back in three weeks for the spirometry result, the slot will be sent.
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): And if something changes before that? And Saturdays, do I keep skipping the water tablet? Purple inhaler stays the same?

[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you cough blood, get much more breathless, or the phlegm changes sharply, come sooner, don't sit on it. Seretide stays two puffs twice a day. Take the 2.5 mg water tablet when you get to your daughter's, so Saturday isn't a miss.
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): Okay. Uh, thanks. I'll try not to google it all night.

spec.situation: Former smoker who quit last year with a long-standing morning cough and brown phlegm; weight stable; no chest pain; spirometry planned; vaccination advice.

traps.happens: A caregiver or relative reports observations ('the cut healed in five days', 'she sleeps badly', 'he does not take the tablets on Sundays'); the patient agrees, disagrees or corrects one point. The nurse also reports a measurement that the patient mentioned before.
traps.label_rule: reported_by follows who said it. A healing cut that healed normally is a negative finding (no slow-healing wounds) or nothing, NOT a symptom. A disputed fact is recorded with certainty disputed or as an uncertainty. A correction replaces the earlier value (Saturday, not Sunday).

features: colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

bad.reason: Medication, dose, indication supported; frequency isn't every morning because Saturday was missed and changed to take later.

bad.reason: Saturday omission was clarified and addressed; uncertainty was resolved, not unresolved.
bad.text: He misses the water tablet on Saturdays, so it is unclear whether the daily dose is taken as prescribed. (type=adherence_uncertain, related_entities=medications[0], resolution_status=unresolved)

omissions.text: Medication adherence detail is recorded wrongly as unresolved uncertainty: the patient and doctor clarified he misses bendroflumethiazide on Saturdays, not Sundays, and the plan was to take the 2.5 mg dose when he gets to his daughter's so Saturday is not missed.

omissions.text: Patient reported a home pulse oximeter reading of 93% and asked if that meant hospital was needed; nurse said home oximeters can drift.
Blue inhaler salbutamol use was described as 'when I'm wheezy' and maybe twice a week; the doctor stated this was a modest amount of use.
Doctor stated that COPD is not cancer and explained COPD as narrowed airways after years of smoking, with cough/phlegm being the bronchitis side.
Doctor said spirometry is already booked and that the patient will be sent an appointment slot.
Doctor explicitly said a chest x-ray was not being ordered today.
Patient denied sleep problems, saying he sleeps fine, gets up once to use the toilet, and then goes back to sleep; the recorded symptom only notes poor sleep as caregiver-reported and disputed.
No blood pressure was measured today; nurse specified that only weight, pulse, and oxygen were checked this morning.
